title: I believe
hook: a creed from credo, I believe: a short summary said together for centuries

segments.voice: Yesterday, ecumenism, and a village called Taizé, the end of the family of churches. Your line was that they may be one. What did you find you share with someone? Day two hundred ninety-seven.

Rome, around the year 200, as an early church handbook describes it. It's the night before Easter, and a woman is standing waist-deep in water, about to be baptized. She's spent months, maybe years, learning. Now the bishop asks her three questions. Do you believe in God the Father Almighty? I believe, she says, and she goes under the water. Do you believe in Christ Jesus, the Son of God? I believe, and under again. Do you believe in the Holy Spirit, and the holy church? I believe. A third time. She comes up, dripping, into a new life. Those questions, asked at the water, grew over time into a short statement that many churches still say every week. Today we begin a new part of the path: what Christians believe. And today's word is the shape it comes in.
screen: `ROME, THE NIGHT BEFORE EASTER.` → `THREE QUESTIONS AT THE WATER.` → `I BELIEVE. I BELIEVE. I BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: Creed comes from the Latin credo, I believe, the first word of the creed in Latin. Some language historians link credo to an old phrase meaning to put your heart on something. So believing, in this word, isn't only agreeing with an idea. It's setting your heart on someone. In the West, the shorter creed is the Apostles' Creed. There's a lovely old legend that the twelve apostles each wrote one line of it, on the day of Pentecost. It isn't true; historians trace it instead to those baptism questions in Rome, slowly shaped over centuries. But it does carry the apostles' faith. In the English of the old prayer book it begins: "I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth." Then it goes to Jesus: born, suffered, crucified, died, buried, descended, rose, ascended, and coming again. Then the Holy Spirit, the church, the communion of saints, forgiveness, the resurrection of the body, the life everlasting. Early Christians called a creed a symbol, from the Greek symbolon, a token broken in two, whose halves fit together to prove who you were. Say the creed, and you show which family you belong to. Not every Christian uses creeds: Quakers keep no set creed, and some Baptists and Churches of Christ say they have no creed but the Bible, while holding much of the same faith. For the next two weeks, we'll walk the creed line by line. Each day, one phrase, and what Christians mean by it. We'll start tomorrow with the first thing it says about God.
screen: `CREDO: TO SET YOUR HEART ON.` · `NOT WRITTEN BY TWELVE APOSTLES.` · `A SYMBOL: A TOKEN BROKEN IN TWO.` · `LINE BY LINE, FOR TWO WEEKS.` · then, large: `I BELIEVE IN GOD THE FATHER ALMIGHTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: two words, with a hand on your heart. Settle, and breathe. Rest a hand on your chest, where the old phrase put belief. Say, quietly: I believe. Notice how the words sound in your own voice, and what comes to mind after them. If you pray, you can go on with the creed's first line: I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth. If you don't, just let the two words rest under your hand. The bell holds the time.
Creed. From the Latin credo, I believe. A short summary of faith said together for centuries.
Your line: a token broken in two. Today, notice what shows people which family you belong to, the thing that proves it. Day two hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Many churches say the Apostles' Creed at baptisms and at morning and evening prayer, and the Nicene Creed at the main Sunday service, with the whole congregation speaking together.

original.note: Latin: I believe, the creed's first word. Often traced to an old phrase meaning to put your heart on something.

trapdoor: what you thought: a creed is a list of rules to agree with.
what it means: a short summary of faith, said together, that began as questions at baptism.
what a scholar hears: credo, likely from a root meaning to set your heart. and symbolum: a broken token whose halves fit.

notes: Editor review (282-299 pass): SERIOUS fix: Quakers were listed as saying 'no creed but the Bible', a Restorationist and Baptist phrase; now Quakers keep no set creed, and some Baptists and Churches of Christ say 'no creed but the Bible'. The baptism scene is now framed as described in an early church handbook; cut 'millions every week', 'best-known creed', 'many scholars think' and 'more than fifteen hundred years'; practice changed from reading a whole creed (which repeated day 283) to saying the first two words with a hand on the heart.
Baptismal questions: from the Apostolic Tradition (attributed to Hippolytus, c. 215; authorship and date debated). Script's scene 'around the year 200' is a reconstruction. Confirm.
Etymology: credo is often linked to Proto-Indo-European *ḱred-dʰeh₁- 'to put heart'; script says 'many scholars think'.
Legend of the apostles each contributing a line: Rufinus and later medieval sources; legend on the day of Pentecost is part of the tradition. Confirm.
Symbolum/symbolon as a token of recognition: standard explanation. Confirm.
Non-creedal Christians named without ranking (Baptists vary; Churches of Christ, Quakers).
